Title

You’ve probably heard that niching down is crucial and imperative.
Why? Well, niching down tends to be more polarizing: some people really gravitate to you and your content, while for others it becomes irrelevant.
This might seem like something undesirable because we want more subscribers, we want more people to be interested in us.
But this is a trap many, many, many people fall into.
Because while we do want more leads, what we mainly want is more quality leads.
So, we want to be putting out a message that reaaaaally applies to a percentage of the population, which, by contrast, will reaaaaally not apply at all to the rest.
Let me give you my go-to example:
If you market yourself as an agent for one-arm jugglers, you’re going to do well in that market, trust me.
Think about it. If people see you do only that, they’ll recognize you as an absolute expert. They’ll know you understand their struggles profoundly because that’s the world you’re familiar with.
It’s silly, but it makes sense—most people won’t care, but the people that do have an extremely high likelihood of becoming your subscribers.
So, by now it should be clear—niching down is good. Don’t try to be too greedy; appeal to a specific segment of the population.
But how do we pick that segment?
Well, before we dive into the “how,” let’s quickly break down what a niche actually is.
A niche is basically a specialized segment of the market focused on a particular topic or interest. It’s where your unique expertise, your passion, and market demand intersect.
Finding this sweet spot is both an art and a science.
First step: Look inward. What are your strengths? What specific knowledge or skills do you have that people would actually want to read about? Don’t be afraid to get specific. Generalists are everywhere; specialists stand out.
Next, consider your passions. If you’re genuinely interested in your niche, you’ll be able to write consistently without burning out. Plus, that passion will come through in your writing, which helps you connect with readers.
Finally, look outward. If there’s no demand for what you’re writing, it’s a hobby—not a niche. Do some market research. Are there enough people interested in your topic? What’s the competition like? Sometimes, the best opportunities are in underserved sub-niches within larger markets.
Here are some quick strategies to help you find your niche:
Identify Problems: Every successful newsletter solves a problem. Check forums, social media groups, and review sites to see what issues your audience faces.
Keyword Research: Use tools like Google Keyword Planner or Ubersuggest to see what people are searching for. Look for patterns and gaps in the market.
Competitor Analysis: Study other newsletters in your space. What do they do well? What are they missing? Find a gap and own it.
Trend Analysis: Use Google Trends to assess the popularity of topics in your niche. Some niches are evergreen, while others are seasonal—both can work.
Surveys and Interviews: Don’t guess. Ask your potential audience what they need through surveys or direct conversations.
Validate Your Idea: Before going all in, test your niche with a minimal viable version of your newsletter. This could be a few test issues or a limited launch to get feedback.
Now, that’s a quick survey of what works, but let me drive home some key points.
Remember what we said in the last lesson: people want value. And value is solving one’s problem. It can either be a knowledge problem or a boredom problem.
A knowledge problem is solved with education, a boredom problem is solved with entertainment.
So, the easiest way to find a problem that you can solve is to think: what problems have I solved for myself?
 It’s quite likely you have something that you’re really an expert in. And don’t shy away from a niche because you feel like it’s too specific.
Nowadays people find success by being an expert in a niche within a niche within a niche.
And the truth is that, if that’s what you’re going for, you will have an uncopyable niche. You will very quickly become the go-to expert in your field because you’re basically the only one talking about it.
For instance, I’ve been on Udemy for years and have learned a lot of insights about course creation. 
If I were to start a newsletter, I could either start it about course creation, where there are infinite creators. Or I could start it about course creation on Udemy and how to grow your account on Udemy. I could target my newsletter specifically to Udemy instructors. 
There I’m basically one of the only people talking about it, and I know by experience people very quickly want to listen to my Udemy advice because of this.
So, find a niche where you have solved a problem for yourself already. Only then should you start doing market research, searching trends, etc. 
Now, remember: choosing a niche isn’t a lifetime sentence. You’re not binding yourself in anyway. Don’t be a victim to analysis paralysis and have this process prevent you from taking action. Pick something and start.
Markets evolve, and so do your skills and interests. Your niche today might not be your niche five years from now—and that’s perfectly fine. The key is to start with a clear focus, build authority, and pivot if needed.
So, to wrap it up: niching down is the key to standing out in today’s world where there are plenty of newsletters, especially for basic topics. It’s all about connecting what you’re great at and passionate about with what people actually want to read. When you get that right, you become the go-to person in your space.
In the next lesson, we’ll dive into defining your ideal reader profile—because once you know your niche, you need to know exactly who you’re writing for.

In the last few lessons we’ve been answering a whole lot of questions: who are we going to market, what are we going to market them, what problems are we going to solve etc. 

This is the last lesson on all this planning we have to do and it’s the cherry on top, it’s where we get to decide how much we’re going to charge and how to go about pricing. 

One of the most appealing things of this model is the retainer - once you get a client, you get paid every month, and agency clients tend to average around 6 months of lifespan, which is pretty nice. 

This, as we’ve talked about, means that if you get 3-10 high ticket clients, you’re basically living a pretty nice, comfortable agency life. 

But how much exactly should you charge and how should you go about mentioning the price etc? 

Well, first thing I want to talk about is some econ terminology. In economics there is the notion of price discrimination. 

This is basically the idea that if you could, to maximize your profit you should price discriminate, meaning charge each customer as much as they’re willing to pay. 

This, of course, can’t be done in most businesses. Imagine you grab an item in a store and the cashier told you you have to pay double because it’s worth more for you than another person. Doesn’t work. 

However, in our business model, in a drop servicing business, this works swimmingly. 

So, instead of having a strict, fixed price that you’re going to use with every client of yours, we’re going to try to price discriminate as much as possible. 

This means that, when we’re going through our sales calls and we’re getting information about their business, we’re going to adjust what our retainer is according to their success and their willingness to invest. 

Here the fact that we work with a 2 call model is ideal, because it means we can have the first call where we collect information, and make a decision on the price for the next call. 

Now, let’s talk specifics and look at how much you should expect to be charging. Naturally, it depends on the service you’re going with, but you should know that even from the start you can expect to charge anywhere from a couple hundred to $2,500 a month. 

I know these numbers can seem pretty high, but to a relatively successful business that is convinced you’re bringing them enough value, they won’t be, they’ll make sense. And naturally you’re not going to go for that highest retainer with a client that’s barely making profit. 

Just for reference though, my first client in my agency was a woman who was doing coaching on the side and was quite wealthy with her main job, so she was actually quite happy to pay $2,500 a month. It really can be that easy sometimes. 

However, most of the time you’re probably going to be charging somewhere between $500 to $1,200 a month when you’re starting out. 

Now, there’s a loooot of options here about framing and introducing these prices. 

For starters, nowadays the market is so saturated that it’s pretty hard to sell a service like ours with no guarantee or some special offer unless you have very impressive results. 

So, if your service allows for it, I would recommend you include a guarantee with your offer. 

Again for reference, when I was starting out with my drop servicing business I offered 15 qualified leads within 30 days or they wouldn’t pay me a penny. 

Now, if you know a bit about lead generation you know that 15 qualified leads is really not a lot, and that doesn’t necessarily mean they’ll get their money back, but it was enough to feel like a security net and make it seem like I was very confident in my abilities. 

A lot of services don’t necessarily favor this sort of guarantee offer, so there is something else you can consider for every service: paid trials. 

Paid trials are essentially a midpoint between a guarantee and a normal retainer. 

It’s essentially a lower investment way to get people to agree to work with you. 

The idea is simple - they pay you a lower fee the first month for you to set everything up and deliver some results, and then starting the second month they pay you full price. 

I’m not a big fan of free trials at all, but this sort of pricing can work pretty well. 

Another thing you can do which, again, depends on the service but can be really nice is a revenue share model. 

This means that you get a cut of whatever revenue you generate for your clients. 

This can, of course, be risky, as you might not get anything from the revenue share if you don’t get results. 

But it inspires a lot of confidence in your clients knowing that you have skin in the game, and if you get them good results it could make you a lot of money as well. 

For reference, in the beginning of my agency I offered
$1,200 upfront
Or $800 upfront and 6% of the revenue I generated
Or $500 upfront and 12% of whatever I generated for them. 

Alright, well there are a few ways to price your services and strategies to frame pricing in a manner that will make clients feel confident, at ease, and like the investment is not too much of  a risk or a jump.

Remember to gauge as much as you can from your initial call with your clients so you can see how much you can price discriminate. and don’t be afraid to propose higher retainers if it seems like it would make sense.

This lesson is important. 

Not necessarily because objection handling is going to get us countless clients, but also because of the implicit lesson it reveals. 

We often think about sales as a binary thing: people either want our product/service or they don’t. 

But the reality is that a good amount of people will be sure that they want nothing to do with you straight away and there’s nothing you can do about those, sure. 

Then, a very small fraction of your lead list will immediately resonate with your offer and feel like it’s exactly what they were looking for. These are nice when they happen, and they usually lead to some smooth, easy sales.

However, as nice as those are, the vast majority of your prospects will fall somewhere in between: they’re not completely closed to the opportunity, but they’re not quite sure that whatever you’re offering makes sense for them. It’s your job to convince them. 

Naturally, that’s what our offer, niche, ICP, and sequence are designed to do, but it might not be enough. 

Every now and then you’ll get people responding to your emails who seem to fall in this middle category. Don’t get me wrong, it’ll sound like they’re almost on the “absolutely not” side of the spectrum, but there will be some sliver of hope, some window of opportunity that we can capitalize on and turn them back into the bright side. 

This will vary a lot. If you’re proposing FB ads as the ultimate solution to their business, some will hit you as “my clients don’t use FB ads.” And others will simply ask “what’s your strategy with FB ads exactly?” So, as I said, it varies. 

Now, I propose that you use a certain framing when it comes to these that will help you with your overall sales game––not only when responding to emails, but also when you’re on sales calls, when you’re interacting with clients etc. 

The frame to adopt is the following: as long as they’re interacting, they still want to be convinced. 

Think about it, everyone wants to be convinced that whatever you have is going to make their life better in a meaningful way. But obviously, not every time we’ve purchased something in our lives it’s served whatever we had in mind, so people are skeptical. 

This is not to say that when people say, “STOP MESSAGING, TAKE ME OFF YOUR LIST” you should try to convert them into a client. And people will say that. 

Anyways, hopefully by now you’re convinced that people expressing and voicing their objections is a window of opportunity. Now let’s look at how to capitalize on it.

Responding promptly
It’s easy to fall into the trap of thinking that people are thinking about our product or service a lot because we are, but in reality their interest is ephemeral, and lasts very little.
Responding as quick as possible will ensure that their interest is still there for you, making it more likely that they’ll respond and entertain the conversation
Acknowledging their concern
One of the main things with dealing with objections is not being confrontational, but as understanding as possible. 
It’s a good idea to empathize with their objection, and possibly say that other prospects of yours in the same niche commonly have the same doubts or concerns.
Isolate Objection
Then, it’s a good idea to reword their objection in a way that isolates it. This is more effective over a call but you can still use this technique over email. Something like “So if I were to show you that FB ads are an effective way to reach your target audience, you’d be more open to the idea of hopping on a call together?”
Provide contextual evidence
Here you want to use case studies of yours or statistics to show that, in fact, this concern they have is not grounded in reality.
Reframe objection
If you use your evidence effectively, you can end up revealing that where they saw a concern, there’s actually an opportunity.
So still with the FB objection, you could say something like “so as you see [statistics] of your target audience uses FB regularly, so FB ads could be an extremely effective way to reach your audience, maybe one that your competition hasn’t thought about!”
Call to action
Finally you want to close with that CTA that leads them towards a call with you. 
Something like “I’m happy to tell you more about this over a quick call. Just 15 minutes, worst case scenario you’ll leave with some new ideas.”
Following up
There’s a good chance, particularly if you don’t respond immediately, that the prospect won’t respond to your email. 
If that happens, simply follow up 24-48 hours later. 
If they don’t respond to that, it’s time to let them go. It’s sad, but that’s also a skill you have to build––you can’t win ‘em all. 

So, at the end of the day your sales coming from objection handling won’t necessarily be life changing, at least from what I’ve seen. 

But dealing with them is still an important tool to have in your arsenal.

Again, it’s important to remember that most prospects will be somewhere in the middle of the spectrum, and it’s our job, through all the tactics we’re learning, to convince them that working together is in their best interest. 

Objection handling is just another way to do that.

Why?

Because it’s personalized. This isn’t sent to everyone in mass or is some corny icebreaker that you’ve seen in your inbox countless times. 

So, in the next few lessons we’re going to look out how to personalize emails. 

The ultimate way to do this would be to go through every one of your leads’ websites, compile some information, and then shape your emails around the information you’ve acquired for every lead.

Newsletter Subscription Trap: "Hey [Name], I noticed you don't have a newsletter sign-up on your website. Have you thought about starting one to engage your audience more effectively?"

Competitor Activity Trap: "Hello [Name], I saw that your competitor [Competitor] recently launched a new feature. Are you planning anything similar?"

Social Media Engagement Trap: "Hi [Name], I noticed your Instagram page is active, but you’re not using LinkedIn much. Have you considered leveraging LinkedIn for your business?"
Newsletter Subscription Trap: "Hey [Name], I noticed you don’t have a newsletter sign-up on your website. Have you thought about starting one to engage your audience more effectively?"
SEO Performance Trap: "Hi [Name], your site isn't ranking as highly as it could for [Keyword]. Have you considered implementing an SEO strategy?"
Competitor Activity Trap: "Hello [Name], your competitor [Competitor] recently launched a new feature. Are you planning anything similar?"
Content Strategy Trap: "Hello [Name], you haven’t published new content recently. Do you need help developing a content strategy?"

Hopefully, the idea is clear. There are too many potential examples for every product or service, but with these examples and concepts, you may find a suitable strategy for your situation.

Remember, this approach may not always be the best. However, in some cases, you might develop a personalized trap that suggests you have researched their brand.

Thus, one of the keys to effective cold emailing is personalizing your emails so they feel like tailored messages rather than broad sequences.

Though basic, this can be useful, particularly when you’re starting.

More refined tactics will be covered in future lessons.
